source: Stanford Encyclopedia: Imre Lakatos (SEP entry)
finding: A programme is theoretically progressive if each new theory has excess empirical content, and empirically progressive if some of it is confirmed. Failing either makes it degenerating.
numbers: No quantitative threshold is given. Case studies only: Newton/Halley (about 72 years), Copernicus (parallax found 1838, nearly 300 years after 1543).
quote: The negative heuristic forbids us to direct the modus tollens at this 'hard core'.
limits: The entry reports no formal empirical test of the method. Evidence is historical case studies and anecdote.
agent_relevance: Gives a precise two-part test for patching: does each patch predict something new, and did any of it come true?

source: SEP Lakatos: novelty is comparative
finding: A prediction counts as novel only if neither rival programmes nor conventional wisdom predicted it. Zahar's amendment: novel if no rival predicts it and it was either unknown or not what the core was built to explain.
numbers: Example: Mercury's perihelion counts as novel for Einstein under Zahar, although it was known for decades.
limits: Zahar's version is use-novelty; it lets old facts count, which blurs the progressive/degenerating line.
agent_relevance: Define new for a patch as: not used to build the patch. Matches guardrail G3 (a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: SEP Lakatos: tolerance of anomalies and appraisal vs advice
finding: Lakatos separated appraisal from advice. The method can label a programme degenerating but does not tell anyone to drop it. Persisting is allowed if the weakness is admitted.
numbers: Examples tolerated: Mercury anomaly under Newton for decades; Bohr programme with an inconsistent core quarantined.
limits: The SEP text itself marks the rationality of persisting as an open question.
agent_relevance: A stop-patching rule must be added by us; Lakatos gives a signal, not a threshold.

source: SEP Lakatos: Urbach IQ case study reversed
finding: Urbach judged the environmentalist IQ programme degenerating relative to the hereditarian one. The Flynn effect (1987), about 13 years later, reversed that verdict.
numbers: About 13 years between verdict and reversal.
limits: One case. Shows a degenerating label can be wrong when judged over a short window.
agent_relevance: Short-window degeneration calls are unreliable; require a minimum number of patches or a rival before stopping.

source: SEP Lakatos: criticisms (Feyerabend, Kuhn, Hacking, Musgrave)
finding: Critics say rational reconstruction fits history to the theory, and no historical process resembles the proposed comparison. Hacking read it as a tool for historians, not a rule for working scientists.
numbers: None.
limits: Contested interpretation; no agreed way to test it.
agent_relevance: Do not treat the label as ground truth; treat it as a counted signal.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia: Scientific Progress
finding: Kuipers allows a new theory to be refuted yet progressive if it has more empirical successes and fewer counter-examples than the old one. Vickers argues novel predictions have been historically unreliable evidence.
numbers: None.
limits: Critiques of the cumulative definition: new theories often correct the old one's predictions.
agent_relevance: Compare success and failure counts between old and patched version, not just whether the patch passes.

source: Branahl (2026, v3) Stagnant Lakatosian Research Programmes
finding: Adds a third category, stagnant, between progressive and degenerating. Four criteria: pure theorizing, no rival, benign epistemic limits, high scientific value.
numbers: Four criteria. Examples from fundamental physics; no sample counts.
quote: why not wait a bit longer?
limits: Philosophical argument; the criteria are not validated empirically and numeric time limits are left to each discipline.
agent_relevance: Separates no progress because of external limits from no progress because the idea is bad. For the agent: no new evidence available is not the same as degeneration.

source: Feyerabend (1975) as cited in Branahl: waiting objection
finding: The 'intermittently empirical problem shift' test is empty because it lets one wait indefinitely.
numbers: No time bound.
limits: Cited via Branahl, not read in original.
agent_relevance: Any stop rule needs an explicit budget; Lakatos supplies none.

source: Branahl on Lakatos's patience and Horgan (1996)
finding: Stagnation is natural in fields where experiments become inaccessible (Horgan's ironic science). Lakatos intended patience, not hasty abandonment.
numbers: None.
limits: Argument, not data.
agent_relevance: Guards against a stop rule that fires too fast.

source: Johansson & Matsubara (2011) String Theory and General Methodology
finding: By Lakatos's criterion string theory is degenerative: facts were known in advance, no new testable predictions, and mismatches drove development (a multiverse added after a failed fit). Yet both giving up and persisting can be defended as rational under Lakatos.
numbers: Qualitative; no counts.
quote: Lakatos has not given us any effective methodological rule by which we could arbiter between rational and irrational actions.
limits: Authors note Lakatos gave no effective rule to arbitrate; he died before answering this.
agent_relevance: A concrete example of a patch (multiverse) added only to save the core, predicting nothing new.

source: Johansson & Matsubara: Hacking's reading
finding: Hacking's defence: the give-up rule is advice to the historian reconstructing history, not to the working scientist, who lacks the information to judge alternatives.
numbers: None.
limits: Interpretive.
agent_relevance: The agent is the scientist, not the historian: it has little information about alternatives, so the signal must come from cheap local counts.

source: Meehl (1990) Appraising and amending theories: the strategy of Lakatosian defense
finding: Meehl: shield the core with auxiliary changes only if the theory has a track record (money in the bank) and the core has high verisimilitude. Seen only in a secondary summary snippet.
numbers: Not available (PDF fetch blocked).
limits: Not read in full; secondary summary from search results.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule: allow patching only while past hit rate is good, tighten when it falls.

source: Batista (2025) EGU poster: soil-erosion modelling as a Lakatosian programme
finding: Reads a field as entering a degenerative phase via scientometrics.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Conference abstract; only seen in a search result list.
agent_relevance: Shows scientometric proxies for degeneration have been tried.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: With oracle labels self-correction helps; without them (intrinsic) accuracy falls. GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 (3 calls) -> 74.7 (5 calls); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0.
numbers: Oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5, HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0; GPT-4 HotpotQA 29.0 to 59.0. Intrinsic GPT-4 HotpotQA 49.0, 49.0, 43.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5, 88.0, 90.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and changes correct to wrong more often than wrong to correct.
limits: Few benchmarks; all alternative prompts tested in Tables 5 and 6 also lowered accuracy.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: more patch rounds without an external signal lower accuracy. A degenerating-patch signal: round count rising while score falls.

source: Huang et al.: multi-agent debate vs self-consistency
finding: Debate is no better than self-consistency at equal calls. GSM8K debate 76.7 (round 1), 83.2 (6 calls); self-consistency 82.5 at 3 calls.
numbers: Debate 6 calls 83.2 vs self-consistency 3 calls 82.5.
limits: One model family; GSM8K.
agent_relevance: More rounds of the same kind of patch are not more evidence. Count compute against gain.

source: Olausson et al. (2024, ICLR) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: When repair cost is counted, gains are modest, vary by subset, and are sometimes absent, versus just drawing more i.i.d. samples. The bottleneck is the quality of feedback.
numbers: On APPS GPT-3.5 gains only at the largest budgets. Human feedback lifts GPT-4 repair success from 33.30% to 52.60% overall (competition level 3.67% to 14.67%); 16 participants, 40 failing programs, 25 repair samples each.
limits: Small human study. HumanEval near ceiling for GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Core rule: compare a patch against a fresh restart at equal compute. Repair that fails the comparison is the degenerating signal.

source: Olausson et al.: stronger feedback model unlocks repair
finding: Pairing a weak code model with a stronger feedback model beats both its own i.i.d. baseline and its own self-repair on APPS.
numbers: Code Llama with GPT-4 feedback gains the most on HumanEval.
limits: Cross-model, so not pure self-repair.
agent_relevance: Patch quality depends on who explains the failure; use real failing output (G2) and an independent critic.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? Critical survey
finding: No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except on tasks exceptionally suited to it. It works well when reliable external feedback exists, and large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
numbers: Survey of many papers; three headline conclusions.
limits: Survey of published work; many studies use oracle info or weak baseline prompts.
agent_relevance: Patching is trustworthy when the failure signal is external (tests, tools), not self-judgment.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning
finding: GPT-4 self-critique causes performance collapse in Game of 24, graph colouring and STRIPS planning; a sound external verifier gives large gains, and plain re-prompting with the verifier keeps most of the benefit.
numbers: As backprompts increase, self-critique quality consistently degrades. LLM-as-verifier on Game of 24: accuracy 87.0%, false positive rate 10.4%, false negative 20.7%. Mystery Blocksworld false negative 97.09%.
limits: GPT-4 only; three domains.
agent_relevance: A degenerating loop looks like: more critique rounds, worse answers. Stop and restart or use a code check.

source: Tsui (2026, COLM) Self-Correction Bench: the self-correction blind spot
finding: 14 open non-reasoning models correct an error when it is attributed to the user but not when attributed to themselves: 64.5% average blind spot. Appending 'Wait' cuts it by 89.3%; 5,306 correction traces in fine-tuning cut it by 76.0%.
limits: Non-reasoning open models; injected errors, not only natural ones.
agent_relevance: Present own prior output as external text to the critic (no authorship), consistent with G5.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) SCoRe: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via RL
finding: Reinforcement-learning training improves intrinsic self-correction by an absolute 15.6% on MATH and 9.1% on HumanEval over base Gemini models.
numbers: 15.6% MATH, 9.1% HumanEval.
limits: Requires training; a scaffold alone cannot do this. Only abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Shows the scaffold must substitute for the missing skill with external checks.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflection over episodes with real feedback improves results: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs 80% for GPT-4; AlfWorld +22% in 12 trials; HotPotQA +20%.
numbers: A ReAct-only agent without reflection converges at a hallucination rate of 22% with no sign of recovery.
limits: Uses environment or test feedback; ground-truth-free reflection gave smaller gains.
agent_relevance: Programme-style repair works when each trial brings new real evidence; an agent repeating the same approach plateaus.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine (opened for comparison)
finding: Iterative self-feedback reported gains across tasks, later contradicted by Huang and Kamoi when fair baselines and no oracle are used.
numbers: Specific numbers not extracted this session.
limits: Contradicted by later critical studies.
agent_relevance: Treat early positive self-refine results as likely inflated by weak baselines.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Later solutions in long chains add little: the first round generally holds most correct answers, and later ones contribute minimally and are less diverse. Training cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 for QwQ-32B-Preview at the same accuracy.
numbers: 48.6% token reduction; one trivial question got 13 solutions in 7 distinct strategies.
limits: Open o1-like models; math benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a learned stop: extra patches after the first success are waste. Count distinct strategies, not rounds.

source: Huang et al. (2025) POPPER: agentic sequential falsification
finding: LLM agents falsify hypotheses via sequential tests with strict Type-I error control, six domains, matching human scientists on biology hypotheses at 10x less time.
numbers: 10x time reduction. Other numbers not extracted (abstract and intro read).
limits: Popperian, not Lakatosian: it tests single hypotheses, not sequences of patched theories.
agent_relevance: Gives a statistical way to decide whether a patch's claimed new prediction really holds.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching LLMs to Self-Debug (abstract)
finding: Self-debugging with execution feedback improves by up to 12% on TransCoder and MBPP, and 2-3% (9% hardest) on Spider with code explanation; can match baselines using 10x more samples.
limits: Abstract only; unit-test execution is a real external signal.
agent_relevance: Repair with execution feedback is the positive control for patching.
